translations.title: Make Sense of Data
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will elicit your prior understandings of single-unit scale picture graphs and bar graphs in preparation for upcoming work with scaled bar graphs.
In grade 2, you learned how to draw and label single-unit scale bar graphs and picture graphs and used categorical data presented in graphs to solve simple problems. In this lesson, you revisit the structure of picture graphs and bar graphs, the features of graphs that help communicate information clearly, and the information you can learn by analyzing a graph. You learn that a key is the part of a picture graph that tells what each picture represents.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Interpret picture graphs and bar graphs to generate questions (orally and in writing) about the data
- In grade 2, you learned how to draw and label single-unit scale bar graphs and picture graphs and used categorical data presented in graphs to solve simple problems
- Read category labels, values, and scales before comparing or calculating with a data display.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
Example 2: What could the categories be for this picture graph? Be prepared to explain your reasoning.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Read the title, labels, categories, and scale.
Step 2: Locate the values needed for the question.
Step 3: Compare, add, subtract, or interpret the values as required.
Step 4: State the result in the context of the data.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: reading the wrong category or scale. Check the labels and scale before using the values.
translations.quickSummary: You will elicit your prior understandings of single-unit scale picture graphs and bar graphs in preparation for upcoming work with scaled bar graphs. In grade 2, you learned how to draw and label single-unit scale bar graphs and picture graphs and used categorical data presented in graphs to solve simple problems.

In previous lessons, you reviewed how to create and interpret single-unit scale picture graphs. In this lesson, you learn that a scaled picture graph is a picture graph where each picture represents an amount other than 1. You read, interpret, and answer questions about scaled picture graphs with a scale of 2 and 5, and generate questions that can be answered by these graphs.

translations.title: Choose a Scale
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will consider the advantages and disadvantages of various bar graph scales.
In previous lessons, you created scaled picture and bar graphs with a given scale of 2 or 5. This lesson extends this work to allow you to choose the scale for your bar graph and reflect on the advantages or disadvantages of your choices. Through the work of the lesson, you notice that you can choose a scale based on the numbers in the data set and that the scale can make a graph easier or more difficult to read (MP6).
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Choose an appropriate scale for a bar graph that represents a given data set
- In previous lessons, you created scaled picture and bar graphs with a given scale of 2 or 5
- Read category labels, values, and scales before comparing or calculating with a data display.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Here is a collection of pattern blocks. Mai, Noah, and Priya want to make a bar graph to represent the number of triangles, squares, trapezoids, and hexagons in the collection. Mai says the scale of the bar graph should be 2. Noah says the scale of the bar graph should be 5. Priya says the scale of the bar graph should be 10. Who do you agree with?...
Approach: “What scale did you use for your bar graph? Why did you choose that scale?” (I used a scale of 5 because each amount can be counted by 5. I used a scale of 10 so I don’t have to make as many marks on the scale.)
Example 2: All the third-grade students at school were asked, “What is your favorite time of the year?” Their responses are shown in this table: favorite time of the year number of students winter 24 spring 13 summer 40 fall 22 Use the data from this table to create a scaled bar graph.
Approach: “How did the scale you chose for your graph affect how your graph looked in the end?” (Certain scales make it easier or more difficult to read the data. For example, with a scale of 10, it might be more difficult to read the exact values from the graph.)

translations.title: Answer Questions about Scaled Bar Graphs
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will answer one-step “how many more” and “how many fewer” questions using a scaled bar graph.

In a scaled bar graph, one unit on the graph can represent more than one item. Read the scale first, use it to determine each category value, and then compare the relevant categories.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Read the graph title, category labels, and scale before using the bars.
- Multiply the number of scale units by the value of each unit when necessary.
- “How many more” and “how many fewer” ask for the difference between two category values.
- A subtraction equation can represent the comparison.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A scaled bar graph uses 1 square to represent 5 students. Summer has 6 squares and winter has 3 squares. How many more students chose summer?
Approach: Summer represents \(6\times5=30\) students and winter represents \(3\times5=15\). The difference is \(30-15=15\), so 15 more students chose summer.

Example 2: Spring represents 20 students and fall represents 35 students. How many fewer students chose spring than fall?
Approach: Find the difference: \(35-20=15\). Spring has 15 fewer students.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Read the graph title, categories, and scale.
Step 2: Convert each relevant bar length into its actual value using the scale.
Step 3: Identify the two categories being compared.
Step 4: Subtract the smaller value from the larger value.
Step 5: State the difference using “more” or “fewer” to match the question.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: counting graph units as if each unit represented 1. Always apply the graph’s scale before comparing the category values.
translations.quickSummary: A scaled bar graph may use one graph unit to represent several items. Apply the scale first, then subtract category values to answer “how many more” or “how many fewer.”

translations.title: Multiplication as Equal Groups
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will use scaled picture graphs as an introduction to multiplication as equal groups.
Scaled picture graphs provide an equal grouping context that naturally elicits multiplication. Multiplication expressions aren’t introduced in this lesson so that you spend more time with concrete representations of multiplication before being introduced to the more abstract representation. The next few lessons focus on the meaning and representations of multiplication, not the product.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Build an understanding of multiplication as equal groups
- Represent a situation involving equal groups in a way that makes sense to you
- Read the hour and minute hands separately; for hour and half-hour times, :00 and :30 must match the minute-hand position.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(40+35\) \(45+35\) \(45+36\) \(34+58\)
Approach: “How did you compose new tens as you solved these problems?” (In the second problem I composed a ten from the 2 fives. In the third problem I composed a new ten from the 5 and the 6 and still had 1 leftover.)
Example 2: Elena collected data about the kind of signs she saw on the way home. The data is shown in this picture graph: Represent the number of speed limit signs Elena saw on the way home. Which statement describes the number of speed limit signs Elena saw? Explain your reasoning. There are 3 pictures and each picture represents 1 speed limit sign. There are 3...
Approach: “These drawings show equal groups. How did these drawings help you represent the data in the picture graph?” (The key told us that each picture represented 2 signs and the drawings helped us see the 2 signs. Each group showed 2 signs.)
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the quantities or expressions to compare.
Step 2: Represent or calculate each value accurately.
Step 3: Decide whether one is greater, less, or equal.
Step 4: Write or explain the comparison.
Step 5: Recheck both values before finalizing.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: deciding from appearance instead of actual values. Represent or calculate both quantities before comparing.
translations.quickSummary: You will use scaled picture graphs as an introduction to multiplication as equal groups. Scaled picture graphs provide an equal grouping context that naturally elicits multiplication.

You are then introduced to multiplication expressions as a way to represent the quantities and situations encountered in the lesson.

- Make sense of tape diagrams that represent multiplication

In the diagram, each part is labeled with a 2.)

In this lesson, you connect the structure of drawings, tape diagrams, and multiplication situations to the structure of multiplication expressions (MP7).

- In previous lessons, you represented situations involving equal groups with drawings and tape diagrams

translations.workedExamples:

Approach: Represent both quantities, compare their values, and state the relationship using words, symbols, or a clear explanation.
Example 2: Write a multiplication expression to match each representation. Explain your reasoning. There were 2 packs of water. Each pack had 6 bottles of water.
Approach: “How would the diagram change if the expression was \(5\times4\) ?” (There would be 5 sections instead of 3.) “How would the diagram change if the expression was \(3\times5\) ?” (Each section would be 5 instead of 4.)

translations.title: More Factors, More Problems
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will solve multiplication problems.
You write equations with a symbol for the unknown to represent multiplication problems and then solve the problems. As in the previous lesson, some problems are unknown factor problems which you do not relate to division until a future unit.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Solve multiplication problems
- You write equations with a symbol for the unknown to represent multiplication problems and then solve the problems
- Measurement units must be equal in size and placed or interpreted without gaps, overlaps, or a shifted starting point.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(1\times10\) \(2\times10\) \(3\times10\) \(4\times10\)
Approach: “What pattern do we see as we look at all of the problems? Why is that happening?” (The factor that isn’t 10 goes up by 1 each time. The products increase by 10 because I have one more group of 10.)
Example 2: For each problem: Write an equation with a symbol for the unknown to represent the situation. Find the number that makes the equation true. Show your reasoning. There are 15 plates. Han placed 5 plates on each table. How many tables have plates on them? equation: solution: Lin made 6 sandwiches. She used 2 slices of bread for each sandwich. How many...
Approach: “How are drawings and diagrams useful for finding the solution to the problem?” (You can count the dots in the drawing. The diagram can be used to count by 10.)
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the quantities being combined.
Step 2: Represent each quantity with objects, a drawing, number line, or expression.
Step 3: Write an addition relationship that matches the representation.
Step 4: Find the total using an efficient strategy.

translations.title: Arrange Objects Into Arrays

translations.title: Division Situation Drawings
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will interpret descriptions or drawings of division situations and recognize whether you involve finding an unknown number of groups or finding an unknown number of objects in each group.
You see the two types of division situations side-by-side in this lesson. You understand that division is finding the number in each group or the size of each group and can match division situations to drawings. You learn that the same drawing can match either type of division situation.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules:
Key ideas:
- Interpret and relate drawings and descriptions of division situations
- Understand that a division situation may involve finding an unknown number of groups or finding an unknown number of objects in each group
- Use mathematical attributes such as sides, angles, parallelism, or length—not size or orientation—to justify a classification.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: Find the value of each expression mentally. \(120 + 120\) \(121 + 119\) \(125 + 115\) \(129 + 111\)
Approach: ”Why do you think all of these expressions have the same value?” (Even though each number is changing, the same amount is being added to one number and subtracted from the other number, so the total is the same.)
Example 2: What did you notice about how the students put themselves into groups of 2? What did you notice about how the students put themselves into 2 groups?
Approach: Identify the total and how it is being shared or grouped, represent the groups, divide, and check the quotient.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: Identify the total and the required number or size of groups.
Step 2: Represent the sharing or grouping.
Step 3: Write the division relationship.
Step 4: Find the quotient using an efficient method.

translations.title: Division as an Unknown Factor
translations.explanation:

translations.title: Attributes that Define Shapes
translations.explanation:
Learning goal: You will describe and identify shapes using attributes that define them.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules:

- Quadrilaterals have four sides, but different quadrilateral categories have additional defining attributes.
- Yes-or-no questions about sides, angles, parallel lines, and equal lengths can narrow the possible shapes.
- Rotation, size, or position does not change a shape’s defining attributes.
translations.workedExamples:
Example 1: A mystery quadrilateral has four right angles and two pairs of opposite sides with equal length. What category must it belong to?
Approach: Four right angles are a defining attribute of rectangles, so the shape is a rectangle. If all four sides are also equal, it is also a square.

Example 2: Which question is more useful for identifying a mystery quadrilateral: “Is it tilted?” or “Does it have a pair of parallel sides?”
Approach: Parallel sides are a mathematical attribute; being tilted is only an orientation. Ask about the parallel sides.
translations.stepByStepSolutions:
Step 1: List the possible shape categories.
Step 2: Identify attributes that distinguish those categories, such as right angles, parallel sides, or equal side lengths.
Step 3: Ask or answer a yes-or-no question about one defining attribute.
Step 4: Eliminate categories that do not match the answer.
Step 5: Continue until the remaining category or shape is justified by its attributes.
translations.commonMistakes: Common mistake: using appearance or orientation as if it were a defining attribute. A rotated square is still a square because its side and angle properties do not change.
